title: Critical Reasoning in Verbal Context
tagline: Year 3 — Main conclusions, hidden assumptions, flaws, paradoxes and parallel reasoning in short arguments

introduction.overview: Verbal critical reasoning treats a short passage as an argument. You are asked to find the conclusion, name the assumption, spot a flaw, resolve an apparent contradiction, or pick an argument with the same pattern. All of these start with the same step: separate the conclusion from its supporting statements, then look at the gap between them. Every question type is a different question about that gap.
introduction.placementRelevance: These items appear in the verbal sections of management and campus tests alongside reading comprehension.
introduction.realWorldContext: Assessing a proposal, a news story or an advertisement uses the same questions.

learningObjectives: Identify necessary assumptions with the negation test
Name common flaws (correlation, sample, converse, false cause)
Resolve paradoxes with a reconciling fact

requiredTopics: Critical Reasoning — Strengthen and Weaken Arguments
prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A conclusion is signalled by words like therefore, thus, so, should; premises by because, since, given that.

coreDefinitions: Main conclusion: the claim the rest of the argument supports.
Assumption: an unstated premise the argument needs.
Flaw: an error in the way premises are used to reach the conclusion.
Paradox: two facts that seem to conflict; a resolution gives a fact that makes both true.
Parallel reasoning: another argument with the same logical form, valid or flawed.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Every question is about the same skeleton: premises, a gap, a conclusion. Find the skeleton, then ask which question is being asked of it.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Mark the conclusion. List the premises. State the gap in one line. Then answer the specific question: what fills the gap (assumption), what is wrong with it (flaw), what follows (inference), what explains it (paradox).

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Negation test
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Deny the assumption; the argument fails

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Common flaws
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Correlation as cause; unrepresentative sample; converse; part-whole

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Paradox resolver
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: A fact that explains both observations

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Parallel form
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Copy the logical shape, not the topic
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: No A is B; all C are B; no C is A

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Must be true
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Some books on the top shelf

mainNarrative: To find the main conclusion, look for the recommendation or claim the rest supports. In "Our town's bus service loses money, and passengers are falling. Raising fares will only drive away more passengers. The council should therefore improve the frequency of buses instead", the conclusion is the final sentence. The rest are premises.

An assumption is a bridge. "The school banned phones so that students will pay more attention" assumes that students will pay more attention if phones are not available. Negate it and the ban has no point.

Common flaws: "The last three managers who wore blue ties were promoted, so blue ties lead to promotion" confuses correlation with cause. "No one has proved the product is not the best, so it is the best" treats absence of disproof as proof.

To resolve a paradox, find a fact that makes both observations true. A hospital introduced a scheduling system to cut waiting times, yet waits rose. If the easier booking system brought many more patients, both facts hold.

For parallel reasoning, rewrite each argument in symbols. "No dog is a bird; all sparrows are birds; so no sparrow is a dog" has the form No A is B; all C are B; so no C is A. A hammer-tool-toy argument with the same form is parallel.

deepDiveAspects.title: Converse error
deepDiveAspects.content: All A are B does not give All B are A; "Ravi is educated, so he is a professor" is invalid.

deepDiveAspects.title: Sampling flaw
deepDiveAspects.content: Surveying only people leaving a gym tells you about gym-goers, not about people in general.

solvedExamples.title: Main conclusion
solvedExamples.question: A town's bus service loses money and passengers are falling; raising fares would drive more away. "The council should therefore improve bus frequency instead." Which sentence is the conclusion?

steps.title: Content
steps.explanation: Improve bus frequency instead of raising fares.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: The council should improve bus frequency instead of raising fares

solvedExamples.title: Flaw
solvedExamples.question: The last three managers who wore blue ties were promoted, so wearing a blue tie leads to promotion. What is the flaw?

steps.title: Flaw
steps.explanation: It assumes the first caused the second.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: It assumes that a connection between two events shows that one causes the other

solvedExamples.title: Paradox
solvedExamples.question: A hospital introduced a scheduling system to cut waiting times, yet waiting times rose. What resolves this?

steps.title: Look for
steps.explanation: A fact that makes both true.

steps.title: Fact
steps.explanation: Easier booking brought many more patients.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: The new system made booking easier, so many more patients came
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The system worked but demand grew.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Mark the conclusion, list the premises, state the gap, and only then read the options with the question type in mind.

commonMistakes.mistake: Picking a premise as the conclusion
Choosing an assumption that is too strong

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Eliminate options that are extreme, irrelevant or restate the premise.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: For parallel reasoning, replace nouns with letters.
